title: EdgeCape: Edge Weight Prediction For Category-Agnostic Pose Estimation
claim: Prior methods predict keypoints without structure or with uniform graphs, yielding errors; ours predicts weighted graphs and localizes accurately.
layout: 4 panels in a row: support, two baselines, ours; colored borders
description: A single row of four square photo panels. The first panel, with a red border, shows the support image of a brown horse with numbered red keypoint circles (0-16) connected by a colored skeleton. The next three panels have green borders and show a different dark horse in a field as the query. The second panel (CapeFormer) shows keypoints as isolated dots with no edges. Several are misplaced, and the leg keypoints overlap in a cluster. The third panel (GraphCape) draws an unweighted skeleton whose leg keypoints still collapse together. The fourth panel (EdgeCape, ours) draws a skeleton with varying edge thickness, meaning learned weights, and the keypoints sit correctly on the body and legs. Bright numbered nodes and colored edges draw the eye first. Captions under each panel are cut off at the bottom.
caption: Given a support image, keypoints definition, and skeletal relations (support data) from any category, our model localizes the keypoints on a query image. Previous methods treat keypoints as isolated (CapeFormer [ref]) or use unweighted graphs (GraphCape [ref]). We, in contrast, predict weighted graphs that lead to better localization.
abstract: Category-Agnostic Pose Estimation (CAPE) localizes keypoints across diverse object categories with a single model, using one or a few annotated support images. Recent works have shown that using a pose graph (i.e., treating keypoints as nodes in a graph rather than isolated points) helps handle occlusions and break symmetry. However, these methods assume a static pose graph with equal-weight edges, leading to suboptimal results. We introduce EdgeCape, a novel framework that overcomes these limitations by predicting the graph's edge weights which optimizes localization. To further leverage structural priors, we propose integrating Markovian Structural Bias, which modulates the self-attention interaction between nodes based on the number of hops between them. We show that this improves the model's ability to capture global spatial dependencies. Evaluated on the MP-100 benchmark, which includes 100 categories and over 20K images, EdgeCape achieves state-of-the-art results in the 1-shot setting and leads among similar-sized methods in the 5-shot setting, significantly improving keypoint localization accuracy. Our code is publicly available.
